candidates.headline: JetBrains' 15,000-developer survey puts weekly coding-agent use at 90% and shows the tool market reshuffling inside eight months
candidates.summary: JetBrains published the AI-coding-agent cut of its tenth Developer Ecosystem Survey — more than 15,000 professional developers worldwide, fielded May–July 2026. Ninety per cent use AI coding agents (local or remote/cloud) at least weekly and 68% daily. Tool shares moved sharply in months: Claude Code 39% worldwide (18% in January 2026, 47% in the US, 31% naming it their primary tool), Codex 16% (3% in January, awareness 27%→65%), GitHub Copilot 21% (down from 29% a year earlier, 79% awareness), Cursor 12% (down from 18% in January; steepest fall in China, 28%→16%), OpenCode 7%, Google Antigravity 6% (15% in India), JetBrains AI 9%.
candidates.so_what: It is the freshest large-sample read on how fast the agent tooling stack is churning, which makes any multi-year tool-standardisation commitment a riskier bet than it looked six months ago.
candidates.notes: DD-SOURCE: strongest in-window primary in the pool. SPECTRUM: measures agent-mode and remote/cloud agents explicitly ('local agents or remote cloud agents'), i.e. the middle-to-far end of the spectrum, NOT autocomplete. DATE CAUTION: the page itself renders only 'August 2026'; search reporting on 21 Aug described it as published 'two days ago', hence 2026-08-19 — Phase 3 must confirm the exact day on the source page before printing it.
candidates.chartable_data: Grouped bar or slope chart: seven named agent tools, each with a January-2026 and a May–July-2026 adoption share — Claude Code 18→39, Codex 3→16, Copilot 29→21, Cursor 18→12. A clean rise-and-fall visual, and the single best 'who is actually winning' chart in the pool.

candidates.headline: DX's Q2 2026 benchmarks: the Developer Experience Index falls for the first time while AI spend rises 28-fold
candidates.summary: DX's quarterly benchmark readout across its customer base reports 95% AI adoption measured by telemetry and more than half of merged code now AI-authored. Median pull-request size doubled from 42 to 72 lines between Q3 2025 and Q2 2026; self-reported AI time savings rose from 3.3 to 6.1 hours a week; median quarterly AI spend went from $1.5K to $44K. Against that, the Developer Experience Index fell from 67 to 65 — the first decline DX has recorded — code maintainability rose 3.8% while change confidence dropped 6.1%, and the innovation ratio moved only from 57% to 58%.
candidates.so_what: It is the first dataset showing spend, throughput and developer experience moving in opposite directions inside the same organisations, which is the shape of the budget conversation engineering leaders are about to have.
candidates.notes: DD-SOURCE: the strongest counterpoint thread in the pool — adoption up, spend up 28x, experience down. Published 14 Aug 2026, one day BEFORE the window opens; legitimate for a deep dive that synthesises recent studies but must be dated honestly if cited. Diginomica's 12 Aug write-up (secondary) adds the framing that DX's data locates Atlassian's 'AI efficiency paradox' inside engineering, plus a figure of roughly 20 lost hours per engineer annually from the DXI drop and change-failure rates up 75% for affected teams. SPECTRUM: DX telemetry covers assistant + agent usage without separating them; treat 'AI adoption 95%' as the whole spectrum.
candidates.chartable_data: Four-series indexed line or small-multiples: AI spend (28x), time saved (3.3→6.1 h/wk), PR size (42→72 LOC), DXI (67→65) over the same five quarters. One chart that carries the entire 'more input, less experience' argument.

candidates.headline: DX's year-long study finds AI time savings peak early and then decay for two-thirds of developers
candidates.summary: Brian Houck's analysis tracked more than 500 companies from May 2025 to April 2026. Nearly one in three developers (31.4%) who started in the lowest time-savings band climbed to the highest; 69.7% of those who reached peak savings did so in under two quarters. But 66.1% reported lower savings in the quarters after their peak, and 50.5% of those who peaked within a single quarter never reported that level again. The median engineering organisation sees a 7.8% increase in PR throughput from AI.
candidates.so_what: It reframes AI productivity as something that decays without deliberate practice change rather than something that compounds, which changes how a rollout should be resourced past month three.
candidates.notes: DD-SOURCE: the 'plateau' thread. Pairs directly with the DORA J-curve — one says the dip is temporary, the other says the uplift is too. SPECTRUM: self-reported time savings across all AI tool types; does not separate agent-mode from autocomplete.
candidates.chartable_data: Cohort-decay chart: share of developers still reporting peak-level savings 1, 2, 3 quarters after reaching peak (100% → 49.5% for fast peakers, → 21% for gradual adopters). Or a simple stacked bar of the 31.4% / 69.7% / 66.1% / 50.5% figures.

candidates.headline: DORA prices the AI adoption dip: a J-curve, a verification tax, and a change-failure rate that gets worse before it gets better
candidates.summary: DORA's 'ROI of AI-assisted Software Development' report (v.2026.1), led by Nathen Harvey with Google Cloud Consulting's delta practice, gives engineering leaders a framework for modelling the financial return on AI adoption. It names three causes of the initial productivity dip — the learning curve, the verification tax (the extra effort to check AI-generated code is reliable, secure and architecturally aligned), and pipeline adaptation. The published sample model for a 500-person org assumes a fully loaded salary of $176,000, shows change failure rate rising from 5% to 6% with $344K of negative downtime impact, and lands at roughly 39% first-year ROI, ~$11.6m value against ~$8.4m investment, with an eight-month payback. DORA also cites Stanford research showing 35–40% productivity gains on simple greenfield tasks against 10% or less on complex legacy code.
candidates.so_what: It gives an engineering leader the numbers to pre-agree a planned productivity dip with a finance partner before the metrics turn red six months into a rollout.
candidates.notes: DD-SOURCE. THROUGHLINE CAUTION: DORA's J-Curve was the Issue 11 Lead and Issue 12 QT1. In a deep dive it is a source section, not an anchor, but Phase 2 should note the repetition and Phase 4 should carry a single cross-issue throughline sentence rather than re-introducing it as new. ATTRIBUTION FIDELITY (v3.6): DORA's own labels are 'verification tax' and 'the tuition cost of transformation' — do not invent alternatives and attribute them. DATE: reported as v.2026.1 released 22 Apr 2026; InfoQ covered it 11 May 2026. Phase 3 must confirm the date on dora.dev before printing.
candidates.chartable_data: The J-curve itself: cumulative value against time, dip then recovery, with the three dip drivers annotated. Also a two-bar comparison of Stanford's 35–40% greenfield vs <=10% legacy productivity gain.

candidates.headline: Pragmatic Engineer's 906-engineer survey: 95% use AI weekly, 56% do most of their work with it, and company size decides the tool
candidates.summary: A survey of 906 respondents fielded 27 January – 17 February 2026 found 95% using AI tools at least weekly, 75% using AI for at least half their engineering work, and 56% for 70% or more. Fifty-five per cent regularly use AI agents, rising to 63.5% among staff+ engineers. Tool choice splits hard by company size: at organisations under 10 people Claude Code leads at 75%, at 10,000+ GitHub Copilot overtakes at 56%. Regular agent users are nearly twice as likely to feel excited about AI (61%) as non-users (36%).
candidates.so_what: The size split is the practical finding — enterprise procurement, not engineer preference, is deciding which agent a large org standardises on.
candidates.notes: DD-SOURCE. SPECTRUM: this survey separates 'AI tools' from 'AI agents' explicitly — 95% weekly on tools, 55% regular on agents. That gap is one of the cleanest spectrum illustrations available. Self-selected newsletter audience; skews senior and AI-engaged. Source-diversity note: Pragmatic Engineer was the Issue 20 Leadership Read.
candidates.chartable_data: Two paired bars by company size (<10, 10-100, 100-1000, 1000-10000, 10000+) showing Claude Code share vs GitHub Copilot share — the crossover point is the visual.

candidates.headline: GitKraken's survey puts autonomous AI as a primary way of working at 28%, nearly four times its level nine months earlier
candidates.source_name: GitKraken (2026 State of AI in Engineering report, via GitLens 19 release)
candidates.summary: GitKraken released GitLens 19 alongside its 2026 State of AI in Engineering report, based on 554 developers and engineering leaders. It reports 96.4% of engineering organisations using AI coding tools and 84% of developers reporting higher productivity. The headline movement: the share of developers whose primary way of working is autonomous AI rose from 7.6% to 28% in nine months. GitKraken's framing is that the bottleneck has moved from generating code to understanding, reviewing and merging it.
candidates.so_what: A four-fold rise in developers working primarily through autonomous agents in nine months is the single fastest practice shift in the pool, and it lands squarely on review capacity.
candidates.notes: DD-SOURCE. SPECTRUM: the only source in the pool that measures the far end explicitly — 'primary way of working is autonomous AI'. VENDOR CAUTION: GitKraken sells the review/merge tooling its report says is the new bottleneck; the finding is self-serving and must be attributed as vendor research, and 554 is a small sample. Published 14 Aug 2026, one day pre-window.
candidates.chartable_data: Single dramatic before/after bar: 7.6% → 28% over nine months, alongside the JetBrains and Pragmatic Engineer agent numbers to show the spectrum spread (95% weekly AI use / 55% regular agent use / 28% primarily autonomous).

candidates.headline: Veracode: AI-generated code still fails security checks 44% of the time, and the number has not moved in a year
candidates.source_name: Veracode (2026 GenAI Code Security Report, via Business Wire)
candidates.summary: Veracode's 2026 report, covering more than 100 models across four testing snapshots, puts the average security pass rate at 56% — nearly 44% of generated code carries a known security flaw — while syntax correctness sits near 100%. GPT-5.5 leads at 68%; six models cluster at 50–53%. Coding-specialised models (51%) do no better than general-purpose ones (52%); model size barely matters (large 53%, medium 51%, small 51%). Python passes at 63%, Java at 30%. The earlier Spring 2026 update (24 March) had the figure at 55%, with cross-site scripting at 15% and log injection at 13%.
candidates.so_what: Model capability and model security have decoupled — buying a better coding model does not reduce the security review burden, which makes the review layer a permanent cost line rather than a transitional one.
candidates.notes: DD-SOURCE. Vendor research (Veracode sells application security), but the methodology is published and the multi-snapshot trend is the valuable part. SPECTRUM: measures raw model code generation, i.e. the autocomplete/generation end, not agent-mode with tooling.
candidates.chartable_data: Two-line chart: syntax pass rate (climbing to ~100%) against security pass rate (flat at 45-56%) across the four snapshots — the divergence is the whole story. Plus a horizontal bar by language: Python 63, C# 58, JavaScript 57, Java 30.

candidates.headline: GitClear: four years of commit data show duplication up 81% and refactoring down to a fifth of its 2022 rate
candidates.summary: GitClear's maintainability research analysed 623 million changes from 2023 to 2026 across eight quality signals. Reuse signals fell — cross-file function calls down 35% since 2023, refactoring ('moved' code) from 21% of changes in 2022 to 3.8% in 2026, legacy code maintenance down 74% (1.7% to 0.46%). Risk signals rose — block duplication up 81% (40.3 to 73.0 per million changed lines), within-commit copy/paste up 41%, error-masking constructs up 47%, two-week churn up 15%. Copy/paste now happens roughly five times more often than refactoring, having been the less common choice in 2022.
candidates.so_what: It quantifies the maintenance bill being accrued behind the throughput numbers, which is the argument an engineering leader needs when asked why velocity gains are not showing up in delivery.
candidates.notes: DD-SOURCE. GitClear's own line — 'the throughput is real, but so is the debt it accrues' — is a candidate pull quote. DATE CAUTION: recorded as January 2026 from the source page; the page gave a month without a day, so 2026-01-15 is a placeholder — Phase 3 must pin the exact date or cite it as 'January 2026'. GitClear sells code-analytics tooling; attribute as vendor research.
candidates.chartable_data: Diverging horizontal bar: reuse signals falling (cross-file calls -35, refactoring -82, legacy maintenance -74) against risk signals rising (duplication +81, copy/paste +41, error-masking +47, churn +15). One of the most SVG-ready datasets in the pool.

candidates.headline: Bessemer's survey of AI-forward engineering orgs: 92% use AI for code generation, 60% for agentic development, and half cannot evaluate the output
candidates.source_name: Bessemer Venture Partners (Atlas), with Ramp and Shopify
candidates.summary: Written with Geoff Charles (CPO, Ramp), Farhan Thawar (VP and Head of Engineering, Shopify) and Jessica Popp (Bessemer operating advisor), the piece reports 90% of tech and engineering teams deploying AI in core operations, with adoption by use case: code generation 92%, code-review augmentation 79%, AI product features 75%, documentation 69%, agentic development 60%. Named challenges: evaluating code quality (52% of leaders), measuring productivity gains (46%), managing token costs (38%), security and IP (29%). Shopify routes all AI requests through a central LLM proxy for cost control and usage analytics without mandating a tool, still requires human review on production code, and reports AI-assisted reversion rates matching pre-AI baselines. Ramp runs a tiered release system with a 5,000-customer early-access group and a templated evidence checklist reviewed within 48 hours.
candidates.so_what: It is the clearest published account of the enablement layer — proxy, checklist, review gate — that separates orgs getting value from orgs generating volume.
candidates.notes: DD-SOURCE, and the strongest implementation/case-study material in the pool. SPECTRUM: separates 'code generation' (92%) from 'agentic development' (60%) — a usable spectrum split. Shopify was the Issue 20 Outside In; the reversion-rate claim is Shopify-reported and unaudited.
candidates.chartable_data: Horizontal bar of adoption by use case (92/79/75/69/60) paired with a second bar of the four named blockers (52/46/38/29) — an adoption-vs-friction pair that reads as one figure.

candidates.headline: Meta ships Muse Code, a terminal coding agent that fans work out to parallel sub-agents in isolated worktrees
candidates.summary: Mark Zuckerberg announced Meta's first AI coding agent, Muse Code, in beta — a terminal agent that plans changes, writes code and validates results across large repositories. It runs specialised background agents that persist through a session and build context, and fans large jobs out to sub-agents working in parallel in isolated git worktrees so the developer's working copy is untouched. Meta is competing on price against Anthropic and OpenAI rather than on capability, and the release comes from Alexandr Wang's Meta Superintelligence Labs.
candidates.so_what: A third serious price-competitive entrant in coding agents changes the negotiating position of any org about to sign a multi-year seat contract.
candidates.notes: Week-news, but PRE-WINDOW (5 Aug 2026) — record for Meanwhile only if new in-window traction can be shown, otherwise On the Radar. SPECTRUM: agent-mode with parallel sub-agents, human still initiates and reviews. Corroborated by Bloomberg, CNBC and SiliconANGLE on the same date.

candidates.headline: Perforce: platform-engineering maturity is what separates orgs getting value from AI from orgs that are not
candidates.summary: Perforce surveyed 820 technology professionals. Seventy-three per cent of organisations with mature platform-engineering practices called platform maturity critical or significant to AI success, against 44% of less mature organisations — a 29-point gap. Sixty-six per cent already use AI in infrastructure workflows and 31% report fully autonomous AI implementation. Craig Risi's summary of the conclusion: AI does not remove the need for strong engineering foundations, it amplifies them.
candidates.so_what: It puts a number on the precondition argument — the platform investment made before the agents arrive is what decides whether they pay back.
candidates.notes: DD-SOURCE for the ops/infrastructure end of the lifecycle. SPECTRUM: '31% fully autonomous' is a self-reported claim about infrastructure workflows, not coding — treat the definition as soft and say so. Vendor research (Perforce).
candidates.chartable_data: Two-bar comparison: 73% (mature) vs 44% (less mature) on platform maturity being critical to AI success. Simple and clean for an inset.

candidates.headline: Capgemini's World Quality Report: nine in ten QE functions are working with generative AI, fewer than one in six have scaled it
candidates.summary: Capgemini's annual quality-engineering study reports roughly 90% of organisations piloting or deploying generative AI in the quality-engineering function, 37% with GenAI-augmented workflows in production and 52% still in pilot, but only 15% at enterprise-scale deployment. Generative AI is now the top-ranked skill for quality engineers at 63%, ahead of core QE skills at 60%. Synthetic test data use rose from 14% in 2024 to 25% in 2025.
candidates.so_what: Testing is the lifecycle stage where AI adoption is widest and scaled deployment is rarest, which is where the review-capacity squeeze from AI-generated code lands hardest.
candidates.notes: DD-SOURCE for the testing/QA lifecycle stage. DATE CAUTION: recorded as the 2025-26 edition; the exact publication date was not confirmed on the Capgemini page and 2025-11-01 is a placeholder. Phase 3 must pin the date on the report page or cite it as 'the 2025-26 edition' without a day. The 58.1% 'testing workload has increased' figure circulating in secondary write-ups was NOT traced to a primary source and must not be printed.
candidates.chartable_data: Funnel: ~90% pursuing GenAI in QE → 52% in pilot → 37% in production → 15% at enterprise scale. A four-step funnel that visualises the pilot-to-production gap for the testing stage.

candidates.headline: Deloitte: 11% of organisations have agentic AI running in production; 38% are still piloting
candidates.source_name: Deloitte Insights (Tech Trends 2026 — agentic AI strategy)
candidates.summary: Deloitte's 2025 Emerging Technology Trends study, published as part of Tech Trends 2026, finds 11% of organisations with agentic AI actively deployed in production, 14% with solutions ready to deploy, 38% piloting, 30% exploring, 42% still building a strategy roadmap and 35% with no formal agentic strategy at all. Deloitte frames the progression as augmentation, then automation, then true autonomy — placing almost all current deployment in the first two phases.
candidates.so_what: The pilot-to-production ratio is the honest denominator behind every 'agents are everywhere' headline, and it is roughly one in four.
candidates.notes: DD-SOURCE, and the pool's best counterpoint to vendor adoption numbers. SPECTRUM: this is the cleanest published taxonomy in the pool (augmentation / automation / true autonomy) and should anchor the deep dive's terminology section. Cross-industry, not engineering-specific — say so. Sample size not disclosed on the page.
candidates.chartable_data: Stacked horizontal bar of the adoption ladder: production 11 / ready 14 / piloting 38 / exploring 30. Reads instantly against any 90%+ 'adoption' figure elsewhere in the issue.

candidates.headline: GitHub's own data: over a million coding-agent pull requests in five months, and a research paper on what happens when agents collide
candidates.summary: Octoverse (published 28 October 2025, updated 28 February 2026) reports more than one million coding-agent pull requests created between May and September 2025, 80% of new developers using Copilot within their first week, 43.2 million pull requests merged monthly (+23% year on year), and 4.3 million AI-related repositories. A July 2026 arXiv paper by Xu, Subramanian and Karthik analysing 33,596 agent PRs across 2,807 repositories found 40.2% of repositories had temporally overlapping agent-authored PRs, accounting for 79.4% of all agent PRs; cross-agent pairs conflicted textually 41.7% of the time against 19.8% for same-agent pairs.
candidates.so_what: Running two different vendors' agents on the same repository roughly doubles the merge-conflict rate, which is a concrete argument for standardising on one agent per codebase.
candidates.notes: DD-SOURCE. The arXiv conflict-rate finding is the most directly actionable technical result in the pool and it is genuinely fresh (6 July 2026, revised 7 July). CAUTION: widely circulated secondary claims of '17 million agent PRs per month by March 2026' and '275 million commits per week' come from a personal blog (danilchenko.dev) and were NOT verified against any GitHub primary — do not print them. Octoverse figures above ARE from GitHub's own page.
candidates.chartable_data: Two-bar conflict comparison: intra-agent 19.8% vs cross-agent 41.7% textual conflict rate. Or a single stat tile on the 79.4% of agent PRs that are co-active.

candidates.headline: Anthropic's Economic Index puts Claude Code at about a sixth of code-related conversations and most of them on the top model
candidates.summary: The June 2026 'Cadences' edition of the Anthropic Economic Index reports Claude Code accounting for roughly one-sixth of conversations involving code and technical work, and running on more capable models — 54% of Claude Code sessions use Opus against 10% for chat. Anthropic describes sessions increasingly consisting of long-running agentic tasks. The March 2026 'Learning curves' edition reported coding tasks migrating from augmentative use on Claude.ai toward more automated workflows in first-party API traffic, with augmentation edging back ahead of automation on Claude.ai (52% vs 45% in November data) after automation briefly overtook it in August 2025.
candidates.so_what: Vendor telemetry showing coding work migrating from chat into long-running agent sessions is the clearest available signal of where the usage mix is actually heading.
candidates.notes: DD-SOURCE for vendor telemetry. SPECTRUM: the automation/augmentation split is Anthropic's own taxonomy and maps to the chat-vs-agent axis — useful, but it is one vendor's traffic and must be attributed as such. The 52%/45% November figures come from the March 2026 edition, not June; keep the two editions separate.
candidates.chartable_data: Automation-vs-augmentation share over time for Claude.ai and 1P API, two lines crossing — Anthropic publishes the series.

candidates.headline: Spec-driven development moves from experiment to tooling category, with Spec Kit, Kiro and Tessl taking three different positions
candidates.source_name: MarkTechPost / GitHub Spec Kit / AWS Kiro
candidates.summary: Spec-driven development — writing an executable specification that agents implement against, rather than prompting from scratch — has consolidated into a recognisable tool category. GitHub's Spec Kit, open-sourced in September 2025 and built on John Lam's work, is the most adopted open-source option and supports 30+ coding agents. AWS's Kiro is generally available with an auto-router selecting models per task. Tessl pushes furthest toward spec-as-source, treating the specification as the maintained artefact and the code as generated output.
candidates.so_what: If the specification becomes the maintained artefact, the requirements and refinement disciplines a team already has stop being upstream process and become the product.
candidates.notes: DD-SOURCE for the spec/requirements stage of the lifecycle — but the WEAKEST-SOURCED candidate in the pool. Everything here is from tool-comparison content marketing, not primary vendor or research material. UNVERIFIED AND NOT TO BE PRINTED: the '93,000+ stars', 'v0.8.7 (May 7 2026)' and '3-10x higher first-pass success rate' claims all trace only to aggregator posts. Phase 3 must pin any spec-driven figure to github.com/github/spec-kit, the Kiro product pages or Tessl directly, or the deep dive covers this stage qualitatively with no numbers.

candidates.headline: Dynatrace ships autonomous SRE agents and a no-code agent builder, with the availability window landing in August
candidates.summary: Dynatrace announced additions to Dynatrace Intelligence: an Autonomous SRE Agent that triggers on newly detected problems and decides whether they belong to an existing investigation, a Cloud SRE Agent that coordinates remediation across AWS, Azure and Google Cloud and centralises findings into a single auditable record, and a no-code Agent Builder for customer-specific workflows. The Cloud SRE Agent was immediately available to SaaS customers; the Autonomous SRE Agent and Agent Builder were slated for August 2026.
candidates.so_what: Autonomous remediation arriving as a shipped product rather than a demo forces the governance conversation — who signs off an agent acting on production — into this quarter.
candidates.notes: DD-SOURCE for the ops end of the lifecycle. Announcement is 27 July 2026 (pre-window) with GA stated as 'expected August 2026' — Phase 3 must confirm whether GA actually landed inside 15-21 Aug before this is treated as an in-window event. SPECTRUM: marketed at the autonomous end but with human-governance framing; the press release's own words ('transparent, auditable, and governed') should be used rather than paraphrased.

candidates.headline: Staff+ engineers now have to rebuild by hand the team culture that AI-parallelised work dissolved
candidates.summary: James Socol, a senior staff engineer currently on sabbatical, argues that AI lets engineers ship features solo, and that this removes the three things that made a group a team: shared goals, interdependent work and stability. The collaborative problem-solving that used to transmit norms happens less often, so staff+ engineers have to deliberately reconstruct culture through celebrations, written charters and modelled behaviour rather than relying on it emerging. He draws on Tuckman's stages of group development rather than new data.
candidates.so_what: It names the second-order cost of parallelised agent work — engineers shipping more while feeling more alone — and puts the repair job on staff+ engineers rather than managers.
candidates.notes: IN WINDOW (18 Aug 2026) and one of only a handful of genuinely in-window pieces in this sweep. Also viable for Meanwhile as a 'would have led' item, or as the deep dive's human/organisational counterweight. No quantitative data — it is an essay. Author has no current org affiliation ('on sabbatical'), which weakens the In Practice 'named operator at a real org' test.

candidates.headline: Anthropic's own randomised trial: junior engineers who delegated to AI scored two letter grades lower and finished no faster
candidates.summary: Anthropic ran a randomised controlled trial with 52 mostly junior engineers, all with at least a year of weekly Python use, learning Trio — an async library none of them knew. The AI-assisted group averaged 50% on the follow-up quiz against 67% for the hand-coding group (Cohen's d = 0.738, p = 0.01), described by Anthropic as nearly two letter grades. The AI group finished about two minutes faster, not a statistically significant difference. Within the AI group, participants who asked conceptual questions and hit errors themselves averaged 65%+; those who delegated code generation and debugging averaged under 40%.
candidates.so_what: It turns 'how junior engineers use AI' from a preference into a measurable skill-formation variable that a manager can actually set expectations about.
candidates.notes: DD-SOURCE: the strongest people-side evidence in the pool, and unusual in that the vendor published a result against its own commercial interest. Small n (52) and a single unfamiliar library — say so. SPECTRUM: chat/assistant use, not agent-mode.
candidates.chartable_data: Grouped bar: hand-coding 67% vs AI-assisted 50% overall, then the AI group split by usage pattern — conceptual questioners 65%+ vs code-delegators <40%. The within-group split is the more interesting half.

candidates.headline: AI is removing the rungs junior engineers used to climb, and with them the pipeline of people who can supervise AI
candidates.summary: Alasdair Allan argues that organisations racing to adopt AI coding tools are simultaneously degrading the pipeline that produces people capable of supervising those tools. The piece assembles METR's finding that experienced developers were 19% slower with AI while believing they were 20% faster, Anthropic's 17% mastery gap, Anthropic-reported internal usage of Claude across 59% of daily engineering work against roughly 20% that can be fully delegated, an estimate that 80–90% of engineering questions now go to AI rather than to colleagues, and a test in which zero of fifteen AI-generated pull requests were mergeable on real projects despite passing automated tests.
candidates.so_what: It connects the hiring decision made this year to the review capacity available in three years, which is the levelling and headcount argument in one line.
candidates.notes: DD-SOURCE for the synthesis section. WARNING: this is a secondary aggregation. Every figure it carries must be re-pinned to its own primary before printing — the METR and Anthropic numbers are pinned in this file, but the '59% of daily work / 20% delegable', '80-90% of questions' and '0 of 15 PRs' figures are NOT independently verified here and Phase 3 must locate their primaries or drop them.

candidates.headline: Harvard research finds firms adopting generative AI cut junior headcount while senior headcount barely moves
candidates.source_name: SSRN (Seyed Mahdi Hosseini Maasoum & Guy Lichtinger, Harvard)
candidates.summary: 'Generative AI as Seniority-Biased Technological Change' uses US résumé data covering roughly 62–65 million workers at more than 280,000 firms, identifying GenAI adoption by detecting 'GenAI integrator' job postings. After adoption, junior employment declines at adopting firms relative to non-adopters while senior employment trends stay largely unchanged. The paper was posted 8 September 2025 and last revised 6 June 2026.
candidates.so_what: It is the largest-sample evidence that AI adoption is reshaping the org chart by seniority rather than by size, which is a different planning problem from a headcount cut.
candidates.notes: DD-SOURCE. Working paper, not peer-reviewed — attribute as such. FIGURE CAUTION: secondary coverage reports the effect variously as 'junior hiring down ~80% per quarter at adopting firms' (Forbes) and '9-10% within six quarters' (other write-ups). These are not the same claim. Phase 3 must read the paper itself and take the authors' own stated magnitude, or print the direction without a number. US labour data; UK/ME transfer is inferential.
candidates.chartable_data: Event-study line: junior vs senior employment index at adopting firms, quarters relative to adoption. The paper publishes the series.

candidates.headline: Gartner expects most organisations to run smaller engineering teams by 2029, up from 15% today
candidates.summary: Gartner predicts that by 2029, 60% of organisations will have adopted smaller software engineering teams at scale, up from 15% in 2026, with the restructuring framed as reshaping teams around combined human and AI capabilities rather than as cost-cutting.
candidates.so_what: It is the clearest published forecast that team shape, not team count, is the variable AI is moving — a different conversation with HR than a headcount reduction.
candidates.notes: DD-SOURCE candidate but VERIFICATION BLOCKED: gartner.com returned HTTP 403 to direct fetch, so the 60%/15% figures are search-result reported only and the analyst name could not be confirmed. Under the run's named risk flag this is the same class as the retired payments aggregates. Phase 3 must open the Gartner newsroom page (or a Gartner-published PDF) and confirm both figures and the date, or this candidate is dropped. It is a forecast, not a measurement — never present it as observed data.

candidates.headline: Commonwealth Bank cuts a further 176 technology and engineering roles as its union alleges offshore re-advertising
candidates.summary: CBA proposed cutting 176 technology and engineering roles plus around 100 more across operations, business banking, institutional banking, HR and retail banking. The Finance Sector Union alleged 'fake redundancies', claiming similar roles were re-advertised through CBA's Indian subsidiary; the bank said the India roles were 'separate and unrelated'. CBA denied the cuts followed directly from increased AI use, attributing them to workflow automation, organisational realignment, streamlining and consolidation. CEO Matt Comyn has said AI would be implemented 'at multiple speeds'.
candidates.so_what: A bank cutting engineering roles while explicitly denying AI as the cause is the pattern worth watching — the attribution fight matters more than the number.
candidates.notes: Surfaced by the cross-beat entity sweep. OUT OF WINDOW (10 July 2026) — On the Radar or a throughline sentence at most, not a Meanwhile item. Australian bank; relevance to UK/ME is pattern-level. Do not aggregate this with other bank/payments workforce numbers — that is the retired thread.

candidates.headline: Lloyds Banking Group is hiring for more than 1,000 AI roles in 2026, nearly 300 of them explicitly agentic
candidates.summary: Lloyds announced recruitment for almost 300 agentic-AI-related roles in the coming months as part of more than 1,000 AI roles planned for 2026, with over 700 colleagues already working on AI use cases. It is launching a Level 6 AI Engineering apprenticeship — one of the first from a UK bank — with a 33-person cohort this year. Its AI Academy, opened in January, has recorded over 400,000 course completions and over 65,000 colleagues finishing responsible-AI modules, against a 67,000-strong workforce. Sharon Doherty, Chief People and Places Officer, framed the focus as making AI deliver real benefit in day-to-day roles.
candidates.so_what: The counter-example to the cuts narrative: a large UK bank treating agentic AI as a hiring and training programme rather than a headcount reduction.
candidates.notes: Surfaced by the cross-beat entity sweep on Lloyds (which entered the pool through the 18 Aug outage). OUT OF WINDOW (22 June 2026) but high UK relevance and a useful counterpoint. The '£50m of GenAI benefit last year, doubling in 2026' figure appears in secondary coverage (Computing, Fintech Futures) but NOT on the Lloyds press release fetched here — do not print it without a primary. Note the awkward adjacency Phase 2 should decide on: the same bank hiring 1,000 AI staff and losing app and Faster Payments availability on 18 August.

candidates.headline: Lloyds, Halifax and Bank of Scotland customers locked out for around two hours on 18 August; Monzo failed over to its stand-in system the next day
candidates.source_name: Evening Standard via AOL (Henry Saker-Clark); Yahoo Finance / TechRadar for the Lloyds incident
candidates.summary: On Tuesday 18 August 2026 a technical fault locked Lloyds, Halifax and Bank of Scotland customers out of mobile and online banking for roughly two hours, with over 2,450 Downdetector reports for Lloyds and more than 1,300 across Halifax and Bank of Scotland, about 67% of them app-related; service returned by mid-afternoon. On Wednesday 19 August, more than 3,000 Monzo customers reported problems after midday. Monzo said it had 'moved into our back-up system Monzo Stand-in', under which customers could still send bank transfers, make card payments and withdraw cash while other app features were unavailable, and was rolling out a fix the same day.
candidates.so_what: Two consecutive days of UK retail banking degradation with two visibly different failure responses — one bank simply down, one bank running a published degraded mode — is the clearest available comparison of what designing for graceful degradation actually buys.
candidates.notes: IN WINDOW, both incidents. The strongest week-news item in the sweep and the natural 'would have led' entry for Meanwhile. VERIFICATION GAPS Phase 3 must close: (1) neither bank has published a cause for either incident — say so explicitly and do not speculate; (2) the Lloyds incident is sourced here to Yahoo Finance/TechRadar/press aggregation, and Finextra's two write-ups (newsarticle/48151 and /48264) both returned HTTP 403 — Phase 3 should pin the Lloyds figures to a bank statement, the BBC, or a status page before printing; (3) some reporting links the Lloyds outage to Faster Payments and other reporting says the 18 Aug event was a separate app/online failure from the earlier July Faster Payments problem — do NOT merge them. BINDING PRIOR FACT (state file): no shared cause has ever been published for the 27 July UK multi-bank degradation; this is a separate event and must not be presented as the same story.
candidates.chartable_data: Simple two-day timeline: 18 Aug Lloyds/Halifax/BoS (~2 hours, ~3,750 combined reports) and 19 Aug Monzo (3,000+ reports, stand-in engaged). A timeline-box treatment, or a compare-table of 'down' versus 'degraded' behaviour by capability — transfers, card payments, ATM, statements.

candidates.headline: PagerDuty: 59% of organisations now run AI in operational workflows, but nearly half still require a human before an agent touches a customer-facing system
candidates.summary: PagerDuty surveyed 1,000 business and IT leaders and developers across seven markets. Fifty-nine per cent are actively incorporating AI into operational workflows with another 34% planning to. Human oversight is still deliberately in the loop: 44% require human involvement when AI remediates customer-facing systems and 43% for cross-functional incident coordination, while 62% expect an even mix of human and AI work over the next three years. Organisations that describe themselves as more resilient than a year ago use AI at 63% against 53% for the less resilient. Every respondent agreed post-incident learning needs strengthening; only 48% turn incidents into structured improvement cycles.
candidates.so_what: It is the best available read on where the human sign-off line is actually being drawn for production agents, which is the governance question a head of engineering is being asked right now.
candidates.notes: DD-SOURCE for the ops/incident stage. SPECTRUM: explicitly measures where autonomy stops — the 44%/43% human-in-the-loop figures are the most useful autonomy-boundary data in the pool. Vendor research (PagerDuty sells incident management); the resilience correlation is self-reported and not causal. The '17.8% average MTTR reduction' figure circulating in secondary write-ups was NOT traced to a primary and must not be printed.
candidates.chartable_data: Autonomy-boundary bar: share requiring human involvement by action type (customer-facing remediation 44%, cross-functional coordination 43%), against the 59% who have AI in ops at all. Also the 100%-agree vs 48%-actually-do post-incident gap as a two-bar contrast.

candidates.headline: The keyv and cacheable npm packages were hijacked at the start of August, spreading through a preinstall hook across packages with billions of monthly downloads
candidates.summary: On 4 August 2026 an attacker took over the GitHub account of the maintainer behind keyv and cacheable and published malicious versions of around ten widely used npm caching packages, together representing over two billion monthly downloads. The payload adds a preinstall hook that runs an obfuscated loader before application code, downloads the Bun runtime, executes a second-stage payload, sweeps for credentials, exfiltrates them to attacker-controlled GitHub repositories and persists via IDE config hooks. It then uses stolen credentials to propagate, with trackers reporting between roughly 400 and over 2,200 affected packages and artefacts.
candidates.so_what: The credential-driven propagation means the exposure is not 'did we install the package' but 'did any build agent hold a token' — a delegation question, not a patching one.
candidates.notes: PRE-WINDOW (4 Aug 2026) and no in-window traction was found in this sweep. AUDIENCE-FIT: this is the Issue 10 'Mini Shai-Hulud' class the spec names as a worked rejection — the useful takeaway only lands for someone running the pipeline. On the Radar or Week at a Glance at one line; never an anchor. Affected-package counts vary widely across trackers; if printed, give the range and the source, not a single number.

candidates.headline: Apple patches an actively relevant ImageIO flaw found by Meta's red team
candidates.summary: Apple released security updates addressing CVE-2026-65346, an integer-overflow vulnerability in the ImageIO framework that could allow arbitrary code execution when processing a malicious image, affecting recent iPhones, iPads and Macs. The flaw was reported by Meta's Red Team.
candidates.so_what: A device-fleet patch item, not an engineering decision — the leadership action is confirming MDM coverage, nothing more.
candidates.notes: IN WINDOW but thin, and sourced only to a daily roundup aggregator. Week at a Glance at one line if used at all. Phase 3 must pin to Apple's own security-releases page before printing the CVE number. No evidence of active exploitation was found — do not imply any.

candidates.headline: Monzo's in-house coding agent now authors around one in ten merged pull requests and runs 1,800 tasks a day
candidates.summary: Monzo's engineering blog describes Agent Chip, an in-house agentic tool built to an MVP in roughly three weeks on an MCP gateway architecture with remote infrastructure and integrations across Slack, Linear, GitHub and local environments. It is authoring around 10% of all merged pull requests at Monzo and routinely running more than 1,800 tasks a day, with nearly all Monzo engineers now using at least one coding agent regularly. Guardrails include sandboxed container isolation, an isolated proxy for external communication, per-task access configuration, environment-specific images and secrets isolation. Engineers still review and merge, and the authors state the bottleneck has moved from engineer capacity to reviewer availability.
candidates.so_what: A UK bank publishing agent-authored PR share, task volume and the specific bottleneck it created is the closest thing available to a like-for-like reference point for a regulated engineering org.
candidates.notes: DD-SOURCE, and the single most relevant case study in the pool for this reader — a UK bank, primary-source, with hard numbers and a named bottleneck. Published 13 Aug 2026, two days pre-window. SPECTRUM: agent-mode with human review gate, explicitly NOT autonomous — Monzo keeps engineers reviewing and merging. Also strong as an Outside In candidate (Monzo was Issue 1's Outside In, so no recent repeat) or as the deep dive's case-study section. Self-reported and unaudited; the 10% figure is Monzo's own measurement.
candidates.chartable_data: Before/after of the bottleneck: engineer capacity vs reviewer availability, or a simple stat row — ~10% of merged PRs, 1,800+ tasks/day, ~3 weeks to MVP, near-universal engineer adoption. Pairs naturally with the GitKraken 'review is the new bottleneck' finding and the DX PR-size doubling.

candidates.headline: Visa, Mastercard and around two dozen others form an Agentic Payments Alliance, with loyalty and rewards named as an unsolved problem
candidates.summary: Rain launched the Agentic Payments Alliance on 18 August 2026 with roughly 25 founding members including Visa, Mastercard, Fiserv, Circle, Remitly, Shift4, Sardine, Lithic, Evertec, Episode Six, Chainalysis, Fireblocks, Solana, Avalanche and Uniswap Labs. The alliance will work on shared research and frameworks, test emerging standards for agent identity and authorisation, and advocate on regulatory questions. Its stated open problems include how to authorise an agent to transact, how to detect fraud in agent-initiated payments, and how to extend loyalty and rewards programmes to agent-based transactions. Mastercard's Sherri Haymond: 'The risk in a moment like this is not that the industry moves too slowly — it's that innovation outpaces alignment.'
candidates.so_what: The card networks have now publicly conceded that loyalty and rewards mechanics do not work when an agent is the buyer, which puts a design question directly on the reader's own product surface.
candidates.notes: IN WINDOW (18 Aug 2026), primary-confirmed against both American Banker and Rain's own announcement. The loyalty/rewards angle is the reason this outranks the other agentic-commerce noise for this reader (standing v1.27 loyalty emphasis). CONTEXT: the state file retires the agentic-payments DEEP-DIVE CLUSTER; this is a fresh, dated, primary-sourced news event, not a revival of that cluster, and should be treated as a week-news item. Note also the crowded standards landscape — ACP (OpenAI/Stripe), x402 Foundation, MPP (Stripe/Tempo) — which is the substance of Haymond's alignment line.
candidates.chartable_data: Landscape map of the competing agent-payment standards bodies and their overlapping members (APA, x402 Foundation, ACP, MPP) — Visa, Mastercard and Stripe appear in several. A small process-flow or Venn-style diagram would carry it.

candidates.headline: McDonald's loyalty AI hands a reporter a 515-page file predicting future orders
candidates.summary: A Wired reporter requested their data from McDonald's loyalty programme and received a 515-page algorithmic dossier predicting future purchases. The Loyalty Newswire frames it as part of a roughly $50 billion behavioural-prediction race across restaurant loyalty programmes. The same 17 August issue carried PYMNTS/FIS research on Gen Z treating debit as a daily financial control panel rather than a payment tool, which it presents as a loyalty opening for banks.
candidates.so_what: The prediction layer inside loyalty programmes is becoming visible to consumers and journalists, which changes the data-handling conversation for anyone building card-linked offers.
candidates.notes: IN WINDOW (17 Aug 2026) via the newswire, but sourced at one remove. Phase 3 must locate the Wired original and confirm the 515-page figure and the $50bn framing before either is printed — the $50bn number is the newswire's characterisation, not necessarily Wired's. Standing v1.27 loyalty emphasis satisfied.

candidates.headline: EU AI Act transparency obligations took effect on 2 August while the high-risk regime slipped to 2027 and 2028
candidates.summary: Article 50 transparency obligations — users must be able to recognise when they are interacting with AI, and generated images, audio, video and deepfakes must be labelled — applied from 2 August 2026, with Commission guidelines adopted on 20 July 2026. The AI Office's enforcement powers over general-purpose AI providers also began on schedule. High-risk obligations for stand-alone Annex III systems (hiring, credit scoring, education, critical infrastructure) are deferred to 2 December 2027, and Annex I embedded high-risk AI to 2 August 2028. Non-compliance can reach €15m or 3% of worldwide annual turnover.
candidates.so_what: The near-term obligation is disclosure, not model governance — the heavier compliance work has moved out by more than a year.
candidates.notes: EXCLUDED FROM ANCHORING: EU AI Act Article 50 was a featured anchor in Issues 21-22 and the v1.31 no-repeat-featured-anchor rule bars it from any featured slot in Issue 23, in any slot. On the Radar or a single cross-issue throughline sentence only. The genuinely new information here is the deferral dates for the high-risk regime, which were not in the Issue 21-22 coverage.

leadership_read.headline: A consultant's account of 300 conversations in which enthusiasm decided what evidence an organisation was willing to see
leadership_read.summary: Nikhil Suresh argues that the corporate world's AI enthusiasm has become a decision-making pathology — institutions are changing how they approve projects, hire, evaluate performance and report failure in ways that reward visible adoption over useful outcomes. He reports roughly 300 professional conversations over an 18-month period in which every AI project he observed failed. The piece went to the front page of Hacker News within hours and was picked up by Daring Fireball.
leadership_read.so_what: It is the sharpest available articulation of why an engineering leader's honest 'this did not work' is getting harder to say out loud, which is a governance problem before it is a technology one.
leadership_read.notes: STANDING CANDIDATE carried forward from the Issue 22 state note — never used, outlet clear, lethain excluded this issue by the no-consecutive-outlet rule. NOT for this issue if the deep dive ships (deep dives carry no Leadership Read) — record for Issue 24. FIGURE CAUTION: the author's reported 0% success rate across ~300 conversations is anecdotal and self-reported, and the RAND '80% of AI projects fail' figure that appears in secondary coverage is a separate claim from a separate source; do not blend them.

leadership_read.headline: Atlassian's Teamwork Lab: 89% of executives believe AI makes their organisation faster, 6% can show where
leadership_read.summary: Atlassian surveyed 12,035 global knowledge workers and 173 Fortune 1000 executives in January–February 2026, with 25 Fortune 500 executive interviews. Eighty-nine per cent of executives believe AI increases speed but only 6% can identify clear organisation-wide ROI. Eighty-five per cent of knowledge workers use AI at work; 29% have integrated it into daily workflows. Fifty-five per cent of executives observe AI widening performance gaps between teams, and the top-performing 14% of teams are 5.6x more likely to credit AI with improved planning and 9.4x more likely to report better collaboration. Atlassian puts a $161bn annual 'fragmentation tax' on Fortune 500 companies and reports 77% of executives expecting flatter structures.
leadership_read.so_what: The 89%-to-6% gap is the belief-versus-evidence problem in one line, and Atlassian's finding that AI widens the spread between teams is the more useful half.
leadership_read.notes: DD-SOURCE: this is the origin of the 'AI efficiency paradox' label that DX's Q2 data then located inside engineering (diginomica, 12 Aug 2026). ATTRIBUTION FIDELITY: 'AI efficiency paradox' is Atlassian Teamwork Lab's own term — use it as theirs. Cross-industry knowledge work, not engineering-specific.
leadership_read.chartable_data: The 89% / 6% belief-vs-evidence pair as a single dramatic contrast, and the 85%-use vs 29%-integrated pair alongside it. Two stat tiles or one paired bar.

in_practice.headline: Building an in-house coding agent at a bank, and discovering the bottleneck was never engineer capacity
in_practice.source_name: Monzo (Fabien Deshayes, Engineering Manager; Oli Haley, Senior Backend Engineer)
in_practice.summary: A first-person account from two named Monzo engineers of building Agent Chip from MVP in about three weeks to ~10% of merged PRs and 1,800+ tasks a day, covering the guardrail architecture, the decision to build rather than buy to avoid vendor lock-in, and the discovery that removing the generation constraint simply moved the constraint to review.
in_practice.so_what: It is a journey, not a framework — the three-quality In Practice filter passes cleanly.
in_practice.notes: Passes all three In Practice qualities: named operators at a real org, a journey rather than a framework, technical content at implication level. DOES NOT FIT the current season ('Making technical decisions when not the SME') — this is engineers writing about their own domain. If a Standard Weekly were being written it would need either a season exception or a different piece. Deep dives are exempt from the long-form variety rule, so for Issue 23 this is best used as case-study material, not as a season entry. Duplicated deliberately from the banking_fintech_loyalty beat.

outside_in.headline: What Ramp and Shopify actually built underneath their AI rollouts: a proxy, a checklist and a review gate
outside_in.source_name: Bessemer Venture Partners (Geoff Charles, Ramp; Farhan Thawar, Shopify; Jessica Popp)
outside_in.summary: Named operators at Ramp and Shopify describe the enablement layer behind their AI adoption: Shopify's central LLM proxy routing every AI request for cost control and usage analytics without mandating a tool, human review still required on production code, and reversion rates matching pre-AI baselines; Ramp's tiered release system with a 5,000-customer early-access group and a templated evidence checklist reviewed within 48 hours. Adoption by use case across the surveyed set runs 92% code generation to 60% agentic development, with 52% of leaders naming code-quality evaluation as their biggest problem.
outside_in.so_what: The transferable lesson is that the org owns the enablement layer even when it does not own the model — swap the company name and the argument holds.
outside_in.notes: Passes the transferability test. CONFLICT: Shopify was the Issue 20 Outside In (Zack Deveau, agentic harness) and the argument here — the orchestration layer the org owns is the durable investment — is close to the same thesis. If used, Ramp should carry the section, not Shopify, or the piece moves to deep-dive implementation material instead. Duplicated from ways_of_working.

rabbit_hole.headline: When two vendors' coding agents work the same repository at once, the merge-conflict rate roughly doubles
rabbit_hole.source_name: arXiv (George Xu, Arjun Subramanian, Nithilan Karthik)
rabbit_hole.summary: Using the AIDev-pop dataset of 33,596 agent-authored pull requests across 2,807 repositories, the authors find 40.2% of repositories contain exactly-overlapping agent-authored PR pairs, accounting for 79.4% of all agent PRs; widening the window to a week takes that to 53.4% of repositories and 95.0% of PRs. Testing 747 unique pairs for merge conflicts, cross-agent pairs conflicted 41.7% of the time against 19.8% for same-agent pairs, with 84.4% of conflict-affected files being source code rather than dependencies and roughly 42% of conflicts structural.
rabbit_hole.so_what: It gives an evidence-based reason to standardise on one coding agent per codebase rather than letting teams pick freely.
rabbit_hole.notes: DD-SOURCE. Preprint, not peer-reviewed; open-source repositories only, so enterprise monorepo behaviour may differ. Last rabbit hole was 2026-08-07, so the cadence gate permits one — but deep dives have no rabbit-hole slot, so this is source-section material for Issue 23.
rabbit_hole.chartable_data: Two-bar: 19.8% intra-agent vs 41.7% cross-agent conflict rate, with the 79.4% co-active share as context.
